title: Fencing strategies for private control plane: traffic prioritization and upgrade-safe tenant quarantine
creator: Marcos Ortega
description:
Problem: During control-plane or regional impairments for Dedicated/Private customers we currently either (a) allow noisy tenants to exhaust capacity and push other tenants past SLOs, or (b) perform blunt evictions during upgrades that increase customer impact. We need finer-grained tenant fencing and prioritized traffic shaping that: 1) isolates noisy tenants fast, 2) preserves SLOs for high-priority tenants, and 3) enables rolling upgrades without tenant-visible errors.

Goals: Implement a set of mechanisms operable in Private and Dedicated deployments: lease-based tenant fences in the control plane, per-tenant circuit breakers with multiple degradation tiers, a prioritized load-shedder that is SLO-aware, and an upgrade coordinator that performs safe node drains and tenant-aware sequencing across regions. All mechanisms must be observable from Console and have safe defaults for on-prem.

Non-goals: Re-architecting serving runtime internals or changing model kernel selection. This ticket is orchestration/coordination + policy enforcement, not model-level changes.

Proposed solution:
- Tenant fencing: implement a short-lived lease (control-plane key with TTL) representing a tenant’s control-plane leadership for nodes/agents. When a lease is revoked (manual quarantine or automated by the load-shedder), traffic for that tenant is tagged and routed to degraded stacks or limited ingress tokens. The lease record is stored in the private control plane etcd/coordstore with revision history for audit.
- Circuit breaker service: lightweight sidecar that tracks token consumption and error rates per-tenant and exposes break levels: GREEN (normal), YELLOW (throttled), RED (quarantine). Break decisions use token buckets, recent p99 latency, and cache hit ratios. Breaker actions are configurable per-tenant policy stored in the control plane and can be overridden by SRE.
- Prioritized load-shedding: implement a pluggable policy engine that takes tenant priority, SLO weighting, and request cost estimate (estimated tokens/seq length) to decide which requests to allow when capacity is constrained. Default policy: preserve 90% of requests for tenants with SLO_weighed_priority above threshold; shed low-value background jobs and large-batch long-context generations first.
- Upgrade coordinator: extend the current rolling-upgrade workflow to be tenant-aware. Before draining a worker, the coordinator consults the circuit breaker and in-flight map, marks affected tenants with READONLY/DEGRADED flags, waits for safe drain windows per-tenant, and, if needed, proactively fences tenants to avoid tail-effect regressions.
- Observability + runbooks: add metrics (tenant_breaker_state, tenant_shed_count, fence_revocations, upgrade_drain_waits), console UI badges per-tenant, and a runbook with recovery playbooks and customer-facing status messaging.

Rollout plan: QA on staging clusters (week 1), dogfood on non-customer Dedicated cluster (week 2), opt-in beta for two enterprise customers with SRE coordination (week 3), wide rollout behind feature flag (week 4).

Testing: automated chaos tests that simulate: control-plane partition, region loss, noisy-tenant spike, and rolling upgrade during degraded state. Acceptance tests must show no more than 10% SLO violations for high-priority tenants during a simulated noisy-tenant event when fencing policies are enabled.

Acceptance criteria: 
1) Lease-based fencing implemented and can be triggered via API and Console.
2) Circuit breaker sidecar evaluates and transitions tenants across break levels accurately under load.
3) Prioritized load-shedder reduces SLO impact for priority tenants by >=80% vs baseline in chaos tests.
4) Upgrade coordinator completes rolling upgrades without aborting due to tenant-caused tail latency in >=95% of runs.
5) Metrics and a Console tenant status panel available to SRE/PM.
6) Runbook and customer-facing communication templates shipped.
